topics.title: Design Car Rental System
topics.markdown:
## Problem

Design a car rental system like Zoomcar or Hertz: customers search vehicles by location and date range, reserve them, pick up, return (possibly at another branch) and pay. The key challenges are **inventory availability over time ranges**, pricing as a **Strategy**, and vehicle creation with a **Factory**.

## Requirements

**Functional**
- Search available vehicles by branch, type and `[from, to]` range.
- Reserve, modify and cancel. Pick up and return, with mileage and fuel or charge recorded.
- Price by vehicle type, duration, add-ons (GPS, insurance), late fees and one-way drop.

**Non-functional**
- No overlapping reservations for the same vehicle.
- New vehicle categories and pricing rules plug in without changes to existing code.

## Learn through a concrete example

Mira books a hatchback from Friday 10:00 until Sunday 10:00. Another customer wants the same car starting Sunday at 10:00. Whether that is allowed depends on both time intervals and the preparation buffer. A reservation is a promise about a future interval; a rental is an actual handover with an odometer, fuel level and condition report.

A *half-open interval* `[start,end)` includes its start and excludes its end. Two reservations overlap when `a.start < b.end && b.start < a.end`. Equality at the boundary does not overlap, but cleaning may extend the unavailable interval.

## See the booking lifecycle

![Vehicle identity and promised time are checked before handover.](lessons/lld-6-flow.svg)

*Vehicle identity and promised time are checked before handover.*

![Customer time and vehicle-ready time are distinct values.](lessons/lld-6-failure.svg)

*Customer time and vehicle-ready time are distinct values.*

### Build and calculate

Use `Vehicle`, `Reservation`, `RentalAgreement`, `Inspection` and `RateQuote`. Do not put historical price in a mutable `Vehicle.dailyRate` field. The agreement preserves what this customer accepted.

```java
// Half-open interval rule; validate start < end at construction.
boolean overlaps(Instant aStart, Instant aEnd,
                 Instant bStart, Instant bEnd) {
    return aStart.isBefore(bEnd) && bStart.isBefore(aEnd);
}
```

At ₹1,800 per started 24-hour period, a 49-hour rental is three periods and ₹5,400 before taxes and extras. A calendar-day tariff gives different results around midnight; name the policy rather than accidentally deriving it from integer division. Store pickup timezone when local branch opening hours matter.

## Design details and alternatives

### Key abstractions

| Type | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `Vehicle` (abstract) → `Car`, `SUV`, `Bike`, `EV` | Registration number, type, branch, status |
| `VehicleFactory` | Creates vehicles from a type and attributes |
| `Branch` | Location and the vehicles currently there |
| `Inventory` | `isAvailable(vehicle, range)` and `findAvailable(branch, type, range)` |
| `Reservation` | customer, vehicle, range, add-ons. State: `BOOKED → PICKED_UP → RETURNED / CANCELLED` |
| `PricingStrategy` | `DailyRate`, `HourlyRate`, `SurgePricing`, decorated by `AddOnDecorator` |
| `Invoice`, `Payment` | Final bill including damages and late fees |

### Design decisions & trade-offs

**1. Availability is about time ranges, not a status flag.** A car can be free today and booked next week, so `status=AVAILABLE` is wrong. Store reservations per vehicle in a `TreeMap<LocalDateTime, Reservation>` keyed by start time. To check `[from, to)`, look at `floorEntry(to)` and see whether it ends after `from`. That is O(log n).

**2. Preventing double booking.** Synchronise per vehicle (lock striping with `ConcurrentHashMap<VehicleId, Object>`), then re-check overlap and insert. In a database this becomes an exclusion constraint (Postgres `tstzrange &&`) or a `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` on the vehicle row.

**3. Pricing composition.** Base Strategy (daily, hourly, surge) plus Decorators for add-ons (`InsuranceAddOn(GpsAddOn(DailyRate))`). Each piece is independently testable, and new add-ons don't touch existing classes.

**4. One-way rentals.** On return, the vehicle's branch changes. That affects future availability by location, so search must consider where the vehicle *will be* at `from`, not where it is now. Keep it simple: a vehicle is searchable at the branch of its last reservation's drop-off.

**5. Reservation as a State machine.** You can only pick up a `BOOKED` reservation within the grace window. Late return moves to `RETURNED` with a late-fee line item.

### Ownership, boundaries and invariants

**Central design question:** Availability is an interval constraint for a specific vehicle, not a boolean on a vehicle type.

Vehicle records asset identity and service status; VehicleType groups attributes. Reservation owns a half-open rental interval and quote. RentalAgreement records pickup/return inspection. PricingPolicy, EligibilityPolicy and PaymentPort express changing rules without duplicating lifecycle state.

**Correctness rule:** Confirmed reservations for the same vehicle must not overlap: existing.start < requested.end and requested.start < existing.end. Maintenance intervals also consume availability.

```text
reservation(id,vehicle_id,start_at,end_at,status,quote_version); agreement(id,reservation_id,pickup_reading,return_reading)
```

### State machine and command contracts

```text
QUOTED -> HELD -> CONFIRMED -> PICKED_UP -> RETURNED -> CLOSED; CANCELLED is policy-dependent
```

### End-to-end execution trace

Find suitable vehicles; quote with immutable dates and tariff; atomically reserve an available interval; authorize deposit; confirm; at pickup check licence and vehicle readiness; record odometer/fuel; at return calculate charges from recorded facts and close the agreement.

### Concurrency and recovery walkthrough

Two requests inspect the same free date range. Lock the vehicle schedule or use a database range exclusion constraint; checking then inserting without an authority is unsafe. Process vehicle locks in stable ID order for multi-vehicle reservations.



### Policy choices and extension seams

Assigning a concrete car early simplifies conflicts but reduces flexibility; booking a category requires capacity accounting and later assignment. A policy should calculate fees while the agreement aggregate owns legal transitions.

### Edge cases that change the design

Back-to-back rentals require turnaround time. Time zones and daylight-saving changes affect displayed pickup times; store instants plus location zone. Late returns may conflict with later reservations and require reallocation rather than silently extending a booking.

### Verification and a practical lab

**Topic-specific cases:** Overlap detection; boundary-touching intervals; maintenance block; deposit timeout; late return; duplicate pickup; pricing across a daylight-saving boundary.

**Lab:** Book adjacent intervals [10:00,11:00) and [11:00,12:00), then add a 30-minute cleaning buffer and show which request must change.

### Further reading

- [Java 21 concurrency contracts](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/package-summary.html) — synchronization and executor semantics.
- [PostgreSQL transaction isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html) — database guarantees differ from process locks.

## Work through failure and extensions

If a customer returns the car late, the next confirmed reservation may become unfulfillable. Keep reservation obligations separate from actual vehicle readiness; offer a replacement or flag an exception. Silently extending the earlier reservation's end can hide the conflict.

Two concurrent bookings need interval exclusion at the authoritative allocation boundary. A Java check on each server is insufficient. At small scale, serialize allocation for one vehicle in a transaction; at category-pool scale, enforce capacity over intervals rather than pretending an unassigned category booking owns a specific registration number.

## Practise, then check your reasoning

1. **Does 10:00–12:00 overlap 12:00–14:00?** Not under half-open intervals; add preparation time before deciding physical availability.
2. **Where does a damage charge belong?** On the rental's return inspection/adjustment record, linked to evidence and a pricing rule, not on all future bookings for that car.
3. **Exercise:** submit two overlapping requests simultaneously. One allocation must lose; non-overlapping requests should both succeed. Then add a buffer and show which formerly valid pair becomes invalid.

topics.title: Chat / WhatsApp
topics.concepts: WebSockets, message ordering, delivery guarantees, presence
topics.markdown:
## Problem

Design a chat system like WhatsApp: 1:1 and group messaging, real-time delivery, delivery and read receipts (✓✓), online presence, offline delivery, and history on multiple devices. The core topics are **persistent connections (WebSockets)**, **message ordering**, **delivery guarantees** and **presence**.

## Requirements

**Functional**
- 1:1 and group chat (≤ 1024 members). Text plus media (via object storage).
- Sent ✓, delivered ✓✓ and read receipts. Last seen and online status.
- Offline users receive messages on reconnect, plus a push notification.

**Non-functional**
- Delivery latency < 200 ms when both users are online. No message loss. Per-chat ordering.

**Scale:** 500M DAU and 50B messages/day ≈ 600k msgs/s average, more at peak. Around 100M concurrent connections; at ~100k per gateway box, that's ~1,000+ gateway servers.

## Learn through a concrete example

Alice sends “hello” to Bob while Bob's phone is offline. A socket alone cannot deliver it later; the server needs a durable message and a way for Bob's devices to resume. Distinguish **accepted by server**, **delivered to device** and **read by person**. They are three different acknowledgements.

A **conversation sequence** orders messages within one conversation. A **client message ID** deduplicates retries from the sender. A **delivery cursor** records what a particular device has received; multiple devices can have different cursors.

## See durable delivery and sender retries

![Persist before acknowledging acceptance to the sender.](lessons/hld-6-flow.svg)

*Persist before acknowledging acceptance to the sender.*

![Client identity connects a retry to the original committed result.](lessons/hld-6-failure.svg)

*Client identity connects a retry to the original committed result.*

### Calculate and partition

At 100,000 messages/s and 500 bytes per stored envelope, raw message data grows about 50 MB/s or 4.32 TB/day before media, indexes and replicas. Store media objects separately and send authorized references. Partition message ownership by conversation to make ordering local rather than inventing one global sequence for every user.

## Design details and alternatives

### Architecture

- **Connection gateways** hold WebSocket (or MQTT) connections. A **session registry** (Redis: `userId → gatewayId`) tracks where each user is connected.
- **Chat service** receives a message, assigns a per-conversation **sequence number**, persists it, then routes it to the recipient's gateway (looked up in the registry) via an internal pub/sub or RPC.
- **Message store:** Cassandra/HBase partitioned by `conversationId`, clustered by `seq`. Efficient "messages after seq X" queries.
- **Offline path:** if the recipient isn't connected, the message waits in the store or an inbox, plus a push notification. On reconnect, the client syncs from its last acked seq.
- **Media:** upload to object storage via a pre-signed URL. The message carries the URL (and an encryption key in E2E designs).

### Key design decisions & trade-offs

**1. WebSocket vs. long-polling.** WebSockets give bidirectional, low-overhead messaging, which suits chat. Long-polling is a fallback. Gateways are stateful, so you need draining on deploy and reconnect with resume.

**2. Ordering.** Global ordering is unnecessary and expensive. Order **per conversation** with a server-assigned monotonic seq (a counter per conversation, or a Snowflake ID plus tiebreak). Clients sort by seq, not by device clock.

**3. Delivery guarantees.** Client sends with a `clientMsgId` (for dedup on retry). Server persists, then acks "sent ✓". The recipient's device acks, giving "delivered ✓✓". Read acks travel the same way. That's at-least-once plus idempotent IDs, which gives effectively-once.

**4. Groups.** Fan-out on write to each member's gateway or inbox for small groups. For large groups, write once to the group log and have members pull by seq.

**5. Presence.** Heartbeats every ~30 s update `lastSeen` in Redis with a TTL. Fan presence changes out only to contacts who are currently viewing that chat, to avoid presence storms.

**6. Multi-device.** Each device keeps its own cursor (last seq) and syncs independently.

### Scope, guarantees and sizing assumptions

**Correctness requirement:** Messages have stable IDs and a defined per-conversation order; delivery and read receipts mean different things.

Assume 1 million concurrently connected clients and 50,000 messages/s. At 1 KB/message, ingress is 50 MB/s before replication and group fanout. A 1,000-member group can amplify one message into 1,000 delivery attempts.

### API contracts and data ownership

```text
POST /conversations/{id}/messages with clientMessageId; GET /messages?after=sequence; authenticated WebSocket events and receipt acknowledgements
```

```text
Logical records (outline, not complete DDL):
message(conversation_id,sequence,message_id,sender_id,ciphertext_or_body_ref); device_cursor(user,device,conversation,last_delivered,last_read)

Primary access/partitioning boundary:
conversation_id for ordering; user_id/device_id for connection routing and inbox cursors
```

### Build the architecture in stages

**Stage 3 — Partition and isolate.** Partition around conversation_id for ordering; user_id/device_id for connection routing and inbox cursors. Track ownership with a routing epoch or a database-native partition mechanism. Move virtual buckets or copy/backfill data with a verified cutover, rather than changing a modulo divisor and assuming records move themselves. Isolate bulk/background workloads from the latency-sensitive path and test the busiest tenant independently.

### Trace the critical request

Authenticate session and membership; deduplicate client message ID; persist with conversation sequence; acknowledge durable acceptance; publish delivery events; gateways send to online devices; offline devices catch up using sequence cursors. Read receipts update only after an explicit user/device read signal.

### Deep dive: the decision that changes this system

WebSockets provide a transport, not durable delivery. Reconnect can replay messages and receipts; clients deduplicate by message ID and request gaps. Per-conversation sequencing avoids an unnecessary global order. End-to-end encryption changes searchable metadata, key management and multi-device history design.

### Failure and race-condition walkthrough

A gateway dies after persistence but before client acknowledgement. Retrying the same client message ID returns the original message. A presence cache can be wrong without losing the durable inbox.

### Security, tenancy and lifecycle

### Trade-offs and a starting recommendation

Small groups can fanout on write; very large channels favor shared logs and read cursors. Ordering across two independent conversations is usually unnecessary. Push notification delivery is not a read receipt.

### SLOs, failure drills and lab

Track durable-ack latency, end-to-end delivery latency, reconnect success, missing-message repair, fanout lag and receipt consistency.

**Test matrix:** Reconnect after a lost acknowledgement, duplicate send, device clock skew, group membership change during delivery, gaps in sequence and offline device catch-up.

### Follow-up questions with answers

**What cannot be eventually consistent here?** The operation establishing this guarantee: Messages have stable IDs and a defined per-conversation order; delivery and read receipts mean different things.

**What is the first scaling pressure to test?** Use the actual workload: Assume 1 million concurrently connected clients and 50,000 messages/s. At 1 KB/message, ingress is 50 MB/s before replication and group fanout. A 1,000-member group can amplify one message into 1,000 delivery attempts.

**Which failure would invalidate the naive design?** A gateway dies after persistence but before client acknowledgement. Retrying the same client message ID returns the original message. A presence cache can be wrong without losing the durable inbox.

**Why not introduce every distributed component immediately?** Small groups can fanout on write; very large channels favor shared logs and read cursors. Ordering across two independent conversations is usually unnecessary. Push notification delivery is not a read receipt.

**How would you demonstrate the design works?** Reconnect after a lost acknowledgement, duplicate send, device clock skew, group membership change during delivery, gaps in sequence and offline device catch-up. Keep the expected invariant and recovery outcome visible in the results.

### Further reading

- [PostgreSQL isolation and anomalies](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html).
- [Apache Kafka delivery and transaction design](https://kafka.apache.org/41/design/design/).
- [Redis rate-limiter design](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/use-cases/rate-limiter/) for atomic shared-state examples.

## Work through ordering and presence

Two concurrent senders can each show optimistic local messages, but the server must choose the conversation's committed order. Device clocks are not a reliable total-order authority. Gaps in a receiver's sequence should trigger replay rather than an assumption that missing messages were deleted.

Presence is soft state with expiry: a disconnected mobile app can appear online briefly. Do not make durable delivery depend on a perfectly accurate online flag. End-to-end encryption changes what servers can inspect and index; explain its key/device model separately from transport TLS.

## Practise, then check your reasoning

1. **Does a WebSocket write prove delivery?** No. It may only enqueue bytes locally; require protocol-level evidence for stronger claims.
2. **Can Bob's laptop reuse his phone's cursor?** Not blindly. Device delivery state differs even if read state is shared by policy.
3. **Exercise:** disconnect Bob, drop Alice's acknowledgement, retry the send and reconnect Bob. Assert one durable message and an ordered replay without conflating read and delivery receipts.

topics.title: Spring AI Fundamentals
topics.markdown:
## Problem

Explain Spring AI's foundations: what problem it solves, how its starters and auto-configuration wire up model clients, the core abstractions (`ChatModel`, `EmbeddingModel`, `Prompt`, `Message`, `ChatResponse`), and how configuration lets you swap providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI, Bedrock, Ollama) without changing business code.

## Requirements

- Spring AI's role: portable abstractions, the Spring-style programming model, and integrations (vector stores, MCP, observability).
- Maven/Gradle starters and the auto-configured beans you get.
- Low-level `ChatModel` vs. high-level `ChatClient`.
- Configuring keys, models and default options. Profiles for local vs. prod.
- Testing strategy.

## Learn through a concrete example

A Spring Boot controller receives a question and returns model text. This looks like an ordinary service integration, and that is the right starting point. Spring AI supplies abstractions for model requests, embeddings, tools and related concerns; it does not make the model's statements authoritative or move your business rules into the prompt.

Use Java 21 and the explicitly pinned Spring AI **1.1.8 educational baseline** used by this repository's compile example. This is not a claim that 1.1 is the newest version. Learn the boundaries first, then consult the selected version's documentation when upgrading.

## See the application boundary

![Application validation surrounds the model integration.](lessons/ai-6-flow.svg)

*Application validation surrounds the model integration.*

![A model can respond successfully while answering the wrong question.](lessons/ai-6-failure.svg)

*A model can respond successfully while answering the wrong question.*

### Build the smallest integration

```java
import org.springframework.ai.chat.client.ChatClient;

// Constructor/method excerpt; dependency configuration is supplied by the app.
final class TutorService {
    private final ChatClient client;
    TutorService(ChatClient.Builder builder) {
        this.client = builder.defaultSystem(
            "Explain backend concepts clearly. State uncertainty.").build();
    }
    String explain(String question) {
        return client.prompt().user(question).call().content();
    }
}
```

This excerpt is the provider-call boundary, not a complete secured service. Add input bounds, timeouts, concurrency admission and error mapping outside it. Do not place a provider secret in browser code or commit it in application YAML. The repository's Maven API-contract example checks selected method shapes without invoking a provider.

## Design details and alternatives

### Key concepts and learning objective

**Question to answer:** What does Spring AI provide, and what still belongs to the application?

Spring AI integrates model clients, embeddings, vector stores, tools and advisors with dependency injection and auto-configuration. The framework reduces integration boilerplate; it does not supply product authorization, tenant isolation, business invariants or an evaluation dataset. Provider portability is partial because capabilities differ.

### Architecture and contracts

```text
HTTP input -> authenticated application service -> ChatClient/EmbeddingModel -> provider adapter -> validated domain result -> response

Application contracts (design outline):
AssistantService.answer(Principal,Question); ModelGateway; EvidenceRepository; UsageBudget
```

For these reference fragments use the documented Spring AI 1.1 API family, not an unversioned mixture of 1.x and 2.x. The educational baseline is explicitly versioned; check the linked migration notes before changing dependencies.

### Worked reasoning and capacity example

At 100 requests/s and 3 seconds average provider residence time, Little’s Law suggests about 300 in-flight calls. A large thread pool cannot create provider quota or database capacity; bound concurrency and queue time.

### Java and Spring AI implementation outline

```java
@org.springframework.stereotype.Service
final class AssistantService {
  private final org.springframework.ai.chat.client.ChatClient client;
  AssistantService(org.springframework.ai.chat.client.ChatClient.Builder builder) {
    this.client = builder.build();
  }
  String explain(String question) { return client.prompt().user(question).call().content(); }
}
```

### Design decisions and alternatives

Keep one explicit provider and one basic use case initially. Configure credentials through environment/secret management. Use application interfaces around retrieval and side effects so deterministic tests need no provider account.

### Failure scenario and safe recovery

Auto-configuration fails because a starter, property prefix or bean type does not match the chosen release. Inspect the condition report and dependency tree before adding manual duplicate beans. Never paste a real key into a committed example.

### Security, privacy and provenance

A singleton service bean must not store current-user prompts or mutable conversation state in fields. Per-request builders/specifications should not be shared across callers.

### Hands-on lab and evaluation

**Build:** Create a Java 21 application with a pinned Spring AI BOM, configure one provider via environment variables, add one service and one HTTP endpoint, then replace the model gateway with a stub for tests.

**Measure:** Verify startup without hidden defaults, missing-key behavior, bounded provider concurrency, cancellation and deterministic service tests. Keep framework integration tests distinct from model-quality evaluations.

### Further reading

- [Spring AI 1.1 ChatClient and request APIs](https://docs.spring.io/spring-ai/reference/1.1/api/chatclient.html).
- [Spring AI tool-execution boundary](https://docs.spring.io/spring-ai/reference/1.1/api/tools.html).
- [MCP specification, versioned protocol concepts](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18).
- [Original RAG research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401) and [Transformer research](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) for background rather than framework instructions.

## Build up capabilities deliberately

First use a deterministic stub response to test the controller. Then test one real model request, then structured output, then retrieval, then memory and tools when the product needs them. Adding everything at once makes a failed answer difficult to diagnose.

Keep application-owned concepts such as `Principal`, `ConversationId`, `Evidence` and `RunBudget` independent of a provider's message JSON. This lets you test permission and lifecycle rules without paid inference. Provider-specific options still matter: an abstraction does not make every model support the same schema, tool or streaming features.

## Practise, then check your reasoning

1. **Does Spring AI run a model locally by itself?** No. It integrates with the configured model backend; a local backend is a separate deployment choice.
2. **Can a successful `.content()` response be trusted as a database fact?** No. Verify against authoritative evidence or use a scoped tool.
3. **Exercise:** implement `/explain` first with a stub, then a configured provider. Test blank input, oversized input, unavailable provider and a private-policy question. Record what your service guarantees and what the model still cannot know.
